A healthy diet costs 4.28 PPP dollars a day. 2.7 billion people can’t pay it.

Since 2017 the price of eating well has risen in 166 of 167 countries with data. Yet the share of people priced out of it has fallen to its lowest level in these estimates. This atlas follows that paradox – from global averages to the countries left behind, and to children’s growth.

How is this measured?

The cost of a healthy diet is the price of the cheapest locally available foods that meet dietary guidelines across six food groups. It is converted to PPP dollars so that countries can be compared.

A person is counted as unable to afford it when their income cannot cover this diet plus the basic non-food needs typical for their country’s income group.

The paradox

Prices rose. Fewer people were priced out.

Between 2017 and 2025 the daily cost of a healthy diet rose 46%. Over the same years the share of people who could not afford it fell by 8.3 percentage points. Read on to see how both can be true.

In 2017 a healthy diet cost 2.94 PPP dollars a day. By 2025 it cost 4.28 – 46% more.

The cost of a healthy diet keeps climbing

World, 2017–2025. PPP dollars per person per day.

Yet the share of people who cannot afford it fell, from 41.0% to 32.7%. Affordability depends on income as well as price. 2020, the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, was the only year the share rose.

The share priced out is falling

World, 2017–2025. % of people who cannot afford a healthy diet.

Because the world’s population grew, the number of people fell more slowly – by 14%, against 20% for the share. 2.69 billion people still cannot afford a healthy diet.

Still 2.7 billion people cannot afford a healthy diet

World, 2017–2025. Billions of people who cannot afford a healthy diet.

But the average hides the divide. In South Asia the share fell from 59% to 36%. In Sub-Saharan Africa it rose, from 70.3% to 72.2%.

The world average hides who was left behind

World and two regions, 2017–2025. % of people who cannot afford a healthy diet.

PPP dollars are international dollars adjusted for what money buys in each country. They are not shop prices or exchange-rate dollars.

Where

Unaffordability is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa

In 41 of 147 countries with an estimate for 2025, more than half the population cannot afford a healthy diet. 35 of them are in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Who’s left behind

Sub-Saharan Africa is moving the other way

South Asia made the biggest gain: the share priced out fell from 59% to 36%. Two regions moved the other way: Middle East & North Africa (38.0% to 41.0%) and Sub-Saharan Africa (70.3% to 72.2%).

Income, not price

Same price, different worlds

A healthy diet costs about the same in rich and poor countries. In 2025 it cost 4.05 PPP dollars a day in low-income countries and 4.20 in high-income ones – yet 76% of people in low-income countries could not afford it, against 8.1%.

The plate

What makes a healthy plate expensive

A healthy diet costs a median 3.9 times more than a diet that only fills you up with calories (174 countries, 2021). Animal-source foods, vegetables and fruit make up 68% of the world-average cost.

Fed vs. well fed

Being fed is not the same as being well fed

In 2024 at least 570 million people lacked enough calories in the countries with data – but 2.8 billion could not afford a healthy diet. Far more people cannot afford a healthy diet than go without enough calories. Stunting – children too short for their age – is one of the clearest signs of long-term poor nutrition.

Sources and method

Data

  • World Bank, Food Prices for Nutrition, version 5.0 (July 2026), CC BY 4.0 – cost and affordability of a healthy diet, 2017–2025.
  • World Bank, World Development Indicators – GDP per capita, PPP (current international $), NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.CD (October 2026).
  • World Bank, Country and Lending Groups, FY2027 classification.
  • FAO, FAOSTAT – Suite of Food Security Indicators: prevalence of undernourishment (accessed 15 October 2026), CC BY 4.0.
  • Method: FAO, The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World – cost and affordability of a healthy diet.
  • UNICEF, WHO and World Bank, Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates, country modelled estimates (March 2026).

How to read the numbers

  • World, regional and income-group figures are the official population-weighted estimates, not averages of countries.
  • Food-group costs exist only for 2021, the International Comparison Program price benchmark year.
  • Undernourishment and stunting end in 2024. Undernourishment is a three-year average shown at its middle year.
  • Why different years? Each chart uses the latest year its source covers: affordability and cost 2025, nutrition 2024, and food-group costs 2021. Change over time is shown as lines, from 2017 onwards.
  • Grey on the map means no estimate. Missing values are never treated as zero.
  • All relationships shown are associations across countries, not proof of cause. Correlations (ρ) are unweighted: each country counts once, whatever its population.
  • Country-level patterns describe countries, not individual households.
  • Coverage: 147 of 180 countries have a 2025 affordability estimate. Missing countries include conflict-affected ones such as Sudan and Somalia, so country counts and rankings cover only countries with data.
